name: Old Gold
lede: Old gold is a glossy yellow, named by comparison with the metal; Paterson dates it as a color term to 1879.

sections.title: A name from the metal
sections.body: Paterson's dictionary describes *old gold* as a glossy yellow and dates its first record as a color term to 1879 [1]. The name reads as a comparison with real [[gold]], with the first shine taken down; it sits in the same neighborhood as a glossy [[yellow]], [[mustard]] and [[goldenrod]] [1][2].

sections.title: Two other uses of the phrase
sections.body:
Philip Ball titles a chapter of *Bright Earth* "Old Gold", about the revival of an austere painter's palette [3]. The chapter opens with an epigraph credited to Rubens, advising painters to keep shadows light and warm and to keep white out of them [3]. That is a figure of speech about painting, not a pigment called old gold [3].

The name also turns up in modern art history. Gage reports that Mondrian, in the 1920s, described a hot orange in his scheme as "old gold" [4]. So the label has meant a muted yellow in the dictionary and a strong orange in one painter's studio talk, and a reader should check which one is meant [1][4].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch here is #CFB53B, a yellow of medium lightness and moderate saturation [5]. Screen values for named colors like this are approximations, and the dictionary gives no formula or pigment for the name [1][5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In the ColorHub archive, 118 of 23,781 paintings hold this color across at least 5% of the canvas, as photographed [5]. It peaks in the 1890s, at about 5.5 times the archive's average rate, and the 26 Kalighat pictures from India that match are the strongest single group [5]. Bonnard has the most matching canvases among Western painters, 6 [5]. Almost every match is a highlight, not a shadow color [5].
